findings.issue_text: [BUG] The diff deletes the only declaration of `p` (`p := prometheus.NewRegistry()`) and then uses bare `p` in `NewDualWriter(Mode1, ls, us, p)` and in all five new Mode3 tests, without adding a package-level `p` declaration anywhere in this diff. If no pre-existing package-level `p` exists in the rest test package, every file in the package fails to compile with `undefined: p`, breaking the entire test suite; the removal of the local declaration is only justified by a declaration this diff never shows.

[BUG] TestMode3_Create's error case ('error when creating object in the unified store fails') sets no `setupStorageFn`, so `d.Storage.Create` — the first call in Mode3.Create — hits an empty testify mock and panics with 'mock: I don't know what to return because the method call was unexpected'. The test binary crashes on this subtest instead of asserting the error path; the whole rest-package test run aborts, so the case never verifies the wantErr behavior it claims to cover.

[BUG] TestMode3_Delete's success case sets only a Storage.Delete expectation, but Mode3.Delete spawns a goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.Delete`, which hits the empty mock and panics as an unexpected call. The panic fires asynchronously (goroutine panics kill the process regardless of test completion), crashing the test run for the whole package; the success path of Mode3.Delete is untestable as written.

[BUG] TestMode3_DeleteCollection's success case sets only a Storage.DeleteCollection expectation, but Mode3.DeleteCollection spawns a goroutine calling `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, which panics as an unexpected mock call. Asynchronous panic crashes the test binary during the package run; the DeleteCollection success path cannot pass as written.

[BUG] In Mode3.Create, a Storage.Create failure is recorded with `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though legacy storage was never called. Unified-storage create failures inflate the legacy-duration error metric and are invisible in the storage metric, so dashboards built on these dual-writer metrics misattribute mode-3 failure rates during migration.

[BUG] In Mode3.Update, a Storage.Update failure is recorded with `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of the storage metric. Same misattribution as Create: legacy metrics count failures that never reached legacy storage, hiding unified-storage update failures from the mode-3 metrics.

[BUG] The success-path metric call in Mode3.Delete passes `name` as the third argument (`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`) while every other call in the file passes `options.Kind` for that label position. The kind label of the storage-duration metric is populated with object names for deletes, fragmenting the metric into per-object series (cardinality blowup) and breaking any aggregation that assumes kind labels.

[BUG] The async Legacy.DeleteCollection in Mode3.DeleteCollection records its duration with `d.recordStorageDuration(...)` rather than `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy delete-collection latencies are counted as unified-storage latencies, corrupting both metrics for the delete-collection method during mode-3 rollout.

[BUG] The async Legacy.Update is called with the raw `objInfo` instead of the previous `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` wrapper, so legacy storage recomputes the updated object from its own current state rather than receiving the object actually written to unified storage. When the two stores diverge, legacy receives an object derived from legacy's stale copy (or the update fails validation against the wrong old object), silently writing different data to legacy than what unified storage holds — the exact drift mode-3 is supposed to avoid.

[ADVISORY] The new Mode3 tests assert only returned values and never assert that LegacyStorage was written (the old commented-out test asserted `lsSpy.Counts(...)`), and the legacy writes are now asynchronous so no test observes them. A regression that silently stops legacy writes in mode 3 (the core purpose of the dual writer) passes CI undetected; whoever later relies on mode-3 legacy parity gets no test signal.

[ADVISORY] The async legacy goroutines (Create here; same pattern in Delete ~108-114, Update ~134-141, DeleteCollection ~161-167) drop the previous error logging — legacy failures now only bump a metric counter. During migration, legacy write failures (e.g. the 10s timeout with cause 'legacy create timeout') produce no log line with object identity, so operators investigating legacy/unified drift have no per-request signal to correlate with.

[ADVISORY] Mode3.Delete builds `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", ..., "kind", ..., "method", ...)` but then passes the bare `d.Log` to `klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` instead of `log`, unlike Create/Get/List/DeleteCollection which pass the enriched logger. Downstream unified-storage delete operations log without the name/kind/method keys, so delete requests lose log correlation that all other mode-3 methods have; the next person diffing the four methods has to work out why Delete alone differs.

[ADVISORY] The added block re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod h1:DkxMin+...` verbatim, a line already present three lines above in the same file. The duplicate is dead weight that the next `go mod tidy` / sum-verification pass strips, producing unrelated diff churn in a file that should only change with dependency updates.

[BUG] The async legacy Create goroutine derives its context from the request context (context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)), which net/http cancels as soon as the handler returns, so the 10-second timeout never protects the write and most legacy writes will fail with 'context canceled'. In production request handling, LegacyStorage.Create is cancelled almost immediately after the unified-storage response is sent, so mode 3 silently stops dual-writing to legacy — store divergence that defeats the entire purpose of mode 3 and corrupts the migration path; the metric will show a spike of legacy errors with no log to explain it.

[BUG] The async legacy Delete goroutine derives its context from the already-returning request context, so the 10-second timeout is dead code and Legacy.Delete is cancelled when the handler returns. Objects get deleted from unified storage but remain in legacy storage, producing divergence the mode-3 migration assumes cannot happen; failures surface only as metric deltas.

[BUG] The async legacy Update goroutine derives its context from the returning request context, so Legacy.Update is cancelled once the handler returns despite the 10-second timeout. Updates land only in unified storage while legacy keeps stale content; the migration's dual-write invariant is silently violated on the most frequently exercised verb.

[BUG] The async legacy DeleteCollection goroutine derives its context from the returning request context, so Legacy.DeleteCollection is cancelled when the handler returns. Bulk deletes leave orphaned collections in legacy storage; a later mode transition or legacy read path will resurrect deleted playlists.

[BUG] On Storage.Create failure the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration, recording a legacy duration for a legacy call that never happened. The legacy-duration metric accumulates samples for failed unified-storage creates while the failed storage call itself is never measured, so dashboards/alerts on dual-writer latency report a store that was never touched and understate storage errors.

[BUG] On Storage.Update failure the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration, attributing the failed storage call to the legacy store. Legacy update latency metrics include failures from storage-only errors and failed storage updates are invisible in the storage metric, misdirecting migration debugging.

[BUG] The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine records its duration via d.recordStorageDuration instead of d.recordLegacyDuration, writing legacy latency into the storage metric series. Storage delete-collection latency is double-counted (sync storage call plus async legacy call) and the legacy metric family has no delete-collection samples, so per-store comparison during migration is wrong.

[BUG] Delete's success path passes the object name as the 'kind' label: d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) instead of options.Kind. One Prometheus time series is created per deleted object name on the dual-writer duration metric, causing unbounded label cardinality and eventual scrape/memory pressure in Prometheus.

[BUG] The async legacy Update passes the raw objInfo instead of the updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj} the old code constructed, so Legacy.Update calls objInfo.UpdatedObject against legacy's own old object rather than receiving the exact object unified storage wrote. The object persisted to legacy storage can differ from the unified-storage result (defaults/RV applied by storage are lost, or UpdatedObject fails against a divergent legacy old object), reintroducing exactly the skew the wrapper existed to prevent.

[BUG] Async legacy writes have no ordering guarantee relative to each other: a rapid create-then-delete (or create-then-update) on the same object can execute the legacy goroutines out of order. Legacy delete runs before legacy create, the delete hits NotFound and is swallowed, and the created object is then written to legacy — leaving an object that exists in legacy but not in unified storage, a divergence no code path or test in this diff handles.

[BUG] The goroutine passes the same obj runtime.Object pointer to Legacy.Create while the caller serializes and returns that same object in the HTTP response, with no copy or synchronization. If LegacyStorage.Create mutates obj (e.g., stamps resourceVersion/UID as storage implementations do), it races with the response serialization on the handler goroutine — a data race detectable under -race and a source of corrupted responses.

[ADVISORY] legacyStoreMock{m, l} and storageMock{m, s} wrap the SAME mock.Mock instance, so the new Mode3 tests cannot count calls per store and never assert that LegacyStorage.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection was invoked at all — and the case named "error when creating object in the unified store fails" is actually configured through setupLegacyFn. The defining mode-3 acceptance criterion (writes land in BOTH stores) is unverified: a regression that skips the legacy write entirely (e.g., the context-cancellation bug above) passes this suite; the mislabeled failing case documents the wrong store and breaks the moment the mocks are separated.

[BUG] Legacy write failures are no longer logged: the old code logged 'unable to create object in legacy storage' (and equivalents in Delete/Update/DeleteCollection), while the new goroutines discard the error after bumping a metric. During a mode-3 migration, every legacy divergence (including the cancellation and ordering failures above) is invisible in logs — operators triaging mismatched data get a metric counter with no error message, object name, or kind.

[ADVISORY] Delete installs the bare d.Log into the context (ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)) instead of the enriched log variable with name/kind/method, unlike every other method in the file. Log lines emitted by the underlying storage during delete lack the correlation fields (name, kind, method) that all sibling methods carry, making delete-path logs unjoinable with create/update/list logs when tracing a divergent object.

[BUG] The async Legacy.Create goroutine derives its 10s timeout context from the request-scoped ctx, which is cancelled the moment the HTTP handler returns, so the legacy write fails with 'context canceled' for virtually every request. Mode 3 silently stops mirroring writes into LegacyStorage; the fallback store drifts from unified storage immediately, defeating the purpose of dual-write mode and poisoning any later migration/rollback that assumes legacy is in sync. Same defect recurs in the Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection goroutines.

[BUG] Update passes the raw objInfo to Legacy.Update, dropping the updateWrapper that previously resolved the updated object once and gave both stores the identical object, so the legacy store re-resolves the update against its own old object. Legacy and unified storage can end up with different content for the same object (legacy's UpdatedObject sees a different 'old'), or legacy fails with resourceVersion conflicts; the write-for-write consistency invariant of mode 3 is no longer enforced. This simplification is not traceable to any stated requirement and reverses deliberate prior behavior.

[BUG] On a Storage.Create failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration, recording a legacy-store error and latency for a legacy write that never ran. Migration dashboards and alerting built on these metrics report legacy failures that did not happen and hide the real storage failure, misdirecting the mode-3-to-mode-2 rollout decisions these metrics exist for.

[BUG] On a Storage.Update failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration, attributing the unified-store failure to the legacy store. Legacy error-rate metrics are inflated by unified-storage failures, corrupting the signal used to gate migration progression.

[BUG] Delete passes the object name as the 'kind' metric label (recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)) instead of options.Kind as every other call site does. The kind label becomes unbounded per-object cardinality (one series per object name), which inflates Prometheus series count and breaks any kind-aggregated dashboard; inconsistent with all sibling call sites.

[BUG] The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection outcomes are recorded in the unified-storage metric. Unified-storage metrics are polluted with legacy outcomes while legacy metrics under-report, corrupting migration gating signal.

[BUG] The legacy-write goroutines discard the error from Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection with no log line, removing the error logging the previous synchronous implementation had. When the async legacy write fails (timeout, conflict, outage) operators get no log evidence at all — the stores silently diverge and the divergence is only visible as an aggregate metric delta, making per-object reconciliation impossible.

[BUG] Delete now returns the unified-storage error immediately for every failure including NotFound, removing the previous handling that tolerated NotFound and still deleted the object from legacy storage. Objects that exist only in legacy storage (or whose unified row is not yet visible) become undeletable through the mode-3 API: the client gets an error and the legacy copy is never removed, a behavior/contract regression on the same request that previously succeeded.

[BUG] The goroutine passes the same obj runtime.Object to Legacy.Create concurrently with the caller serializing/returning `created`, with no synchronization between the two goroutines. If the unified storage Create mutates obj in place (as k8s-style storage does when assigning resourceVersion) or the response path touches it while the legacy write reads it, this is a data race detectable under -race and can produce corrupted legacy writes or torn reads.

[BUG] The 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' case sets the failure expectation on the Legacy mock and leaves the Storage mock unconfigured (returning nil, nil), so Storage.Create succeeds, Create returns nil error, and the wantErr assertion fails. The test case either fails outright or, if adjusted later, does not exercise the claimed scenario — a unified-storage Create failure — because in mode 3 a legacy-only failure cannot produce an error; the error path of Create with a failing unified store is never actually tested.

[ADVISORY] The goroutine+WithTimeoutCause+metric block is copy-pasted four times across Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection with observed drift between the copies (wrong metric function in two, name-as-kind in one). Every future mode-3 fix (e.g., the context-cancellation bug or the metric mixups above) must be applied in four near-identical places and history shows the copies already disagree; extracting one helper would have made these four bugs structurally impossible.

[ADVISORY] The rewritten mode-3 tests assert only unified-storage outcomes and never assert any LegacyStorage interaction, dropping the LegacyStorage.Create/Update/Delete call-count assertions the previous (commented) test suite had. The defining behavior of mode 3 — that legacy storage also receives every write — is completely untested, so a regression where legacy writes never happen (exactly what the request-context cancellation bug causes) ships green.

[ADVISORY] Delete wires klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of the request-scoped `log` that carries name/kind/method, unlike every sibling method which uses `log`. Log lines emitted by the unified storage layer during Delete lose the name/kind/method fields present on all other mode-3 operations, making Delete-side storage errors harder to correlate in operational triage.

[BUG] The async legacy-write goroutine derives its 10s timeout from the request context (context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)), so the legacy write is cancelled the moment the HTTP handler returns, and the same pattern is repeated in the Delete (110-116), Update (136-143), and DeleteCollection (163-169) goroutines. Every mode-3 mutation races the legacy write against request-context teardown: once Storage.Create/Delete/Update returns and the handler finishes, net/http cancels ctx, killing an in-flight legacy DB write mid-flight; the object silently never lands in legacy storage, with no error surfaced anywhere.

[BUG] Mode-3 Update passes the raw objInfo to Legacy.Update instead of the updateWrapper{upstream, updated} the previous code built, so the legacy store recomputes the updated object against its own stored old version rather than receiving the object unified storage actually wrote. When legacy and unified storage hold different versions of the object (the normal state during a migration), the legacy write materializes a different result than what unified storage stored — or errors when the object is absent from legacy — permanently diverging the two stores that mode 3 exists to keep identical.

[BUG] The Delete success path passes the object name as the kind label: d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), while every other site passes options.Kind. Every deleted object name becomes a new Prometheus label value on the dual-writer duration metric — unbounded series cardinality on a hot delete path — and the 'kind' label carries a name instead of a kind for those samples, breaking any dashboard that groups by kind.

[BUG] On Storage.Create failure the code records the legacy-duration metric (d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)) instead of the storage-duration metric. Failed unified-storage creates are attributed to the legacy store in metrics, so the legacy latency/error series reports writes that never touched legacy and the storage error rate is undercounted, misdirecting migration-mode debugging.

[BUG] On Storage.Update failure the code records the legacy-duration metric (d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)) instead of recordStorageDuration. Failed unified-storage updates are counted as legacy failures; the storage error-rate series is understated and the legacy series is polluted with storage-path errors.

[BUG] The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine records its result with d.recordStorageDuration instead of d.recordLegacyDuration. Legacy delete-collection latencies and errors are folded into the unified-storage metric family, corrupting both series and hiding legacy-side failures during migration.

[BUG] Mode 3's contract (write to both stores, read from storage) is degraded to fire-and-forget: the legacy write is an at-most-once goroutine with a fixed 10s timeout, no retry, no outbox/reconciliation, and the returned error is discarded (errObjectSt is used only for a metric). Any legacy-write failure — timeout, DB blip, validation rejection — leaves the object permanently absent from legacy with no repair mechanism, so legacy-API consumers see missing/stale data for the rest of the migration window; the old synchronous path surfaced these errors in logs and kept the stores convergent within a request.

[BUG] Delete no longer falls through to Legacy.Delete when Storage.Delete returns NotFound — the old code swallowed apierrors.IsNotFound and still deleted from legacy, the new code returns the storage error immediately. Objects that exist only in legacy storage (created before dual-write started, not yet migrated) can no longer be deleted through the API in mode 3: the call fails with NotFound and the legacy row survives as an orphan that no code path in this design cleans up.

[ADVISORY] Legacy-write failures are no longer logged anywhere: the goroutines discard the error object ("_, errObjectSt :=" / "_, _, err :=") and record only a metric, whereas the old code logged "unable to create object in legacy storage" with the object attached. When the stores diverge, operators get an error-counter bump at best and no log line identifying which object, name, or cause failed — debugging divergence during migration requires reproducing from metrics alone.

[ADVISORY] The literal time.Second*10 legacy-write timeout is copy-pasted at four sites (lines 53, 112, 137, 165) with no named constant, config knob, or statement of provenance. The next editor tuning one copy (e.g. raising DeleteCollection to 30s for batch deletes) silently leaves the other three at 10s, giving different durability guarantees per verb with nothing in review to catch the divergence.

[ADVISORY] The kind label for logs and metrics is read from options.Kind (CreateOptions/GetOptions/DeleteOptions TypeMeta), which the apiserver request handlers never populate — callers construct these options from query params only. Every mode-3 log line and metric sample emitted in production carries kind="", so per-kind dashboards and log filters built on these fields are empty even though the code looks like it records the kind.

[ADVISORY] Delete builds the enriched logger (log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", ...)) but then binds d.Log — the bare logger — into the context: ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log), so the goroutine and any ctx-derived logging lose the name/kind/method fields the other verbs attach. Delete-path log entries emitted from the context lack the object name and method, making mode-3 delete triage inconsistent with create/update/list for the same failure.

[ADVISORY] The new mode-3 tests never assert that the legacy storage was invoked: legacyStoreMock and storageMock share the same mock.Mock instance (so expectations cannot distinguish which store was hit), and mock.AssertExpectations / spy counts are never checked, so the async legacy-write path the diff introduces is effectively unverified. A regression that skips the legacy write entirely (e.g. the goroutine never scheduled, or the whole legacy block deleted) keeps every one of these tests green — the dual-write behavior, the one thing mode 3 exists to do, has no test coverage.

[BUG] Mode 3's contract was silently changed from a synchronous dual-write (legacy errors logged and observable) to a fire-and-forget goroutine whose legacy error is only recorded as a metric and never logged, with no reviewer/human acceptance of the semantic change recorded in this diff. Operators relying on the documented mode-3 invariant ('writes to LegacyStorage and Storage') now get silent divergence: a legacy Create that fails (timeout, validation, conflict) produces no log line at all — the original code logged 'unable to create object in legacy storage' with the object — so legacy/unified drift is invisible except in a metric, and the mode-2→mode-3 migration safety property is quietly lost.

[BUG] The async legacy-write goroutines derive their 10s timeout context from the HTTP request context (ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, ...) at the top of each method), so the 'background' Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection is cancelled almost immediately when the request handler returns, making the 10-second timeout and the async design illusory. Legacy writes/deletes are aborted mid-flight for most requests (context canceled), producing spurious legacy-duration failure metrics and actually reducing legacy-write success rate versus the old synchronous code; the same cancellation also kills re-run validation funcs (deleteValidation/updateValidation) that depend on request-scoped context values, so legitimate legacy writes fail with 'context canceled' errors that no one asked for.

[BUG] The async legacy Update passes the raw objInfo instead of the previously wrapped updateWrapper containing the resolved updated object, so legacy storage re-computes UpdatedObject against its own (possibly stale) old object rather than receiving the exact object the unified store just accepted. Legacy and unified stores receive different updates when their old objects diverge (RV conflicts, divergent fields), and legacy Update can fail validation or write different content than what the client was told succeeded — a silent data-integrity drift that the removed updateWrapper mechanism existed specifically to prevent.

[BUG] Delete no longer falls through to Legacy.Delete when the unified store returns NotFound (the old code explicitly ignored apierrors.IsNotFound and proceeded to delete from legacy), so objects existing only in legacy storage are now undeletable through the mode-3 path. During any real migration from mode 0/1 to mode 3, pre-existing legacy-only objects cannot be deleted via the unified API: the call returns NotFound and the legacy row persists forever, resurfacing in legacy API reads and blocking migration completion; the old behavior cleaned them up as a side effect.

[BUG] The DeleteCollection legacy goroutine calls d.recordStorageDuration instead of d.recordLegacyDuration for the legacy operation, mislabeling legacy delete-collection outcomes as unified-storage metrics. Dual-writer dashboards and migration readiness signals read wrong: legacy DeleteCollection failures/successes are counted in the storage bucket, so a failing legacy path during migration looks healthy and a healthy one looks duplicated; the metric by name is the contract other Grafana migration tooling consumes.

[BUG] In Create (lines 45-47) and Update (lines 129-132), the unified-storage error path records the failure with d.recordLegacyDuration instead of d.recordStorageDuration, misattributing storage failures to the legacy store. Every unified-store Create/Update failure inflates the legacy-duration failure metric and skews per-store latency/failure ratios, corrupting exactly the observability this PR was adding to monitor dual-writer migration health.

[ADVISORY] Delete puts d.Log (without name/kind/method fields) into the context via ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of the prepared log variable, unlike every other method in this file. All structured log lines emitted inside Delete (e.g. 'unable to delete object in storage') are missing the name, kind, and method fields that every sibling method includes, making delete-path logs unfilterable/unjoinable in the dashboards this logging work was built for.

[ADVISORY] The rewritten mode-3 tests deleted the old (commented) assertions that LegacyStorage.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection were each called exactly once, and the new tests never assert any legacy call occurs, so the core mode-3 invariant is no longer covered by any test in this diff. A future regression that drops the legacy write entirely (or breaks it as in the ctx-cancellation bug above) passes the entire suite silently — the tests now verify only the unified-store half of the dual write that this PR exists to establish, giving false confidence in the migration path.

[ADVISORY] Create hands the same runtime.Object to the background legacy Create while the handler serializes it into the HTTP response, so any mutation of obj by the legacy storage path (setting resourceVersion/UID, deepcopy elision) races with the response writer. Under concurrent load the response body can observe a mid-mutation object, and -race runs in CI will flag the dual-writer when legacy storage implementations mutate their input, producing flaky builds and, worst case, corrupted API responses for Create requests.

[ADVISORY] The 10-second legacy timeout and the fire-and-forget goroutine-per-request pattern are hard-coded with no configuration, flag, or metric on goroutine count, so every Create/Update/Delete now spawns an unbounded background goroutine holding the request context and validation closures. Under write-heavy load (e.g. bulk provisioning hitting Create) goroutine count grows with in-flight legacy writes and cannot be tuned or disabled without a code deploy; a slow legacy backend pins request memory and validation closures for up to 10s per write, an operational regression the previous synchronous design did not have.

[ADVISORY] The added go.work.sum block duplicates the line 'github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod h1:DkxMin+qOh1Fgkxfbt+CUfBqqsCQJMG9op8Os/irBPA=' which already exists two lines above the hunk. Duplicate sum entries make future go.work.sum regenerations noisy and can trip consistency checks in tooling that assumes a canonical, de-duplicated sum file; a `go mod tidy`-driven cleanup will churn this hunk again in an unrelated PR.

[BUG] The async Legacy.Create goroutine derives its 10s timeout context from the request context, so when the HTTP handler returns the parent context is cancelled and the legacy write aborts almost immediately — the 10-second timeout is unreachable in the production request path. In mode 3 the legacy write silently fails for essentially every create issued over HTTP (the goroutine records a duration but the error is discarded), so unified storage and legacy storage diverge from day one; rows are missing at migration cutover and the divergence is invisible because no error is surfaced or logged.

[BUG] The async Legacy.Delete goroutine inherits the request context, which is cancelled as soon as the delete handler returns, so the legacy delete is aborted before the 10s timeout can apply. Deleted objects are removed from unified storage but frequently remain in legacy storage (or vice versa if cancellation lands mid-call), producing persistent dual-store divergence on every delete and polluting the legacy-failure metric with cancellation errors.

[BUG] The async Legacy.Update goroutine inherits the request context, which is cancelled when the update handler returns, aborting the legacy update regardless of the 10s timeout. Legacy storage stops receiving updates in the request path, so the legacy copy drifts from unified storage on every write — the exact inconsistency mode 3 exists to prevent during migration.

[BUG] The Delete success metric passes the user-controlled object name as the 'kind' label value: d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) instead of options.Kind used at every other call site. Every distinct object name becomes a new Prometheus label series; a tenant creating/deleting many uniquely-named objects drives unbounded metric cardinality and can exhaust Prometheus/telemetry memory (cardinality-based DoS), and the storage metric series is polluted with object names.

[BUG] The legacy update goroutine receives the raw client-supplied objInfo instead of the resolved, validated object (the previous code wrapped it via updateWrapper with the object actually written to unified storage), so Legacy.Update re-resolves the update against its own possibly divergent old object. The resourceVersion/optimistic-concurrency precondition enforced on the unified-storage write is not applied to the legacy write: a stale update rejected by unified storage can still be applied onto legacy's old state, writing an object to legacy that differs from unified storage and bypassing the concurrency control during the migration window.

[BUG] The DeleteCollection legacy goroutine calls d.recordStorageDuration instead of d.recordLegacyDuration, recording legacy delete-collection outcomes under the storage metric series. Legacy delete-collection latency and failures are misattributed to the storage metric, corrupting the dual-writer dashboards operators rely on to judge migration readiness; legacy failures in delete-collection become invisible in the legacy series.

[BUG] When Storage.Create fails, the error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), recording a unified-storage failure (with the storage timer) as a failed legacy operation. The legacy success-rate metric shows failures for operations that never touched legacy storage; the same miscategorization exists in Update's storage-failure path (line 130), so both metrics misreport and migration health signals are wrong.

[BUG] When Storage.Update fails, the error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), attributing a unified-storage failure and its timer to the legacy metric. Legacy update metrics report failures for writes that never reached legacy storage, distorting the legacy-error-rate signal used to gate the mode 3→2 transition.

[BUG] All six new TestMode3_* tests assert only the value passed through from the unified-storage mock (e.g. `assert.Equal(t, obj, exampleObj)`), and none asserts that LegacyStorage was written, that LegacyStorage reads are NOT used, or that a legacy write failure leaves the request succeeding — the three defining behaviors of mode 3 (the old commented-out test asserted `lsSpy.Counts("LegacyStorage.Create") == 1` and `LegacyStorage.Get == 0`; the rewrite asserts no call counts at all). A mode-3 DualWriter that silently skips the legacy write entirely (or reads from legacy) passes this entire suite; combined with the new fire-and-forget goroutines that only log legacy errors, real legacy/unified data divergence would ship undetected. Checked for coverage: the only test files in the diff touching this subject are dualwriter_mode3_test.go, dualwriter_mode1_test.go (only removed a local prometheus registry) and pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go (black-box CRUD, no legacy-write verification) — no assertion on legacy-side behavior exists anywhere.

[BUG] legacyStoreMock and storageMock are constructed wrapping the SAME `mock.Mock` (`ls := legacyStoreMock{m, l}; us := storageMock{m, s}`), so every expectation is shared between both backends and the tests structurally cannot distinguish which store received a call — in TestMode3_Create's success case only `setupLegacyFn` is registered yet the Storage.Create call is satisfied by that same expectation. Assertions like the test name 'creating an object only in the unified store' are unverifiable by construction: a call routed to the wrong backend matches the same mock and the test still passes. Any future attempt to add per-backend call-count assertions (the one thing mode 3 needs tested) will be meaningless until the mocks are split.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Update's storage-failure path calls d.recordLegacyDuration instead of d.recordStorageDuration, misattributing a failed unified-storage update to the legacy metric (same defect as Create's error path). Unified-storage update failures inflate the legacy failure/latency series, corrupting the migration metrics this dual-writer rewrite exists to produce.

adjudication.rationale: In `DualWriterMode3.Update`, the storage error branch calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the failure occurred in `d.Storage.Update(...)` (unified store) and `startStorage` measures the storage call. This misattributes unified-store failures/latency to legacy metrics. The same misattribution is also visible in `Create`: on `d.Storage.Create(...)` error it calls `recordLegacyDuration(...)` with `startStorage`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The DeleteCollection goroutine calls d.recordStorageDuration for the Legacy.DeleteCollection result; it should be recordLegacyDuration, so legacy bulk-delete outcomes are recorded as storage outcomes. The storage histogram receives two samples per DeleteCollection (one synchronous, one from the goroutine) and the legacy histogram receives none, making the metric lie about which backend produced each sample.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go, DeleteCollection records storage metrics synchronously via d.recordStorageDuration(... startStorage). Then the legacy DeleteCollection is executed in a goroutine, but its result is also recorded with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy) instead of recordLegacyDuration. This misattributes legacy bulk-delete latency/errors to the storage metrics and results in storage being sampled twice while legacy receives no samples for DeleteCollection.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The async Legacy.Update is called with the raw objInfo, dropping the previous updateWrapper indirection that fed Legacy.Update the exact object computed from the unified store's old state. Legacy.Update now re-derives the updated object via objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, legacyOld) using the legacy store's own (possibly divergent) old object, so the legacy write can produce a different result than what was returned to the client or fail outright when the object exists only in the unified store — exactly the drift case mode 3 must survive; the divergence lands in a goroutine that only increments a metric.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go, Update previously computed the updated object once (based on the unified store’s old object) and then ensured Legacy.Update received that exact object via an updateWrapper (the removed block that did Storage.Get + objInfo.UpdatedObject + updateWrapper, and the Legacy.Update call using &updateWrapper{..., updated: obj}). The new code calls d.Storage.Update with the original objInfo, then asynchronously calls d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...) directly. That means Legacy.Update can re-run objInfo.UpdatedObject against the legacy store’s own old state (or fail if legacy is missing/divergent), producing a different object than what unified storage returned to the client—precisely the drift scenario mode 3 should tolerate. The legacy write happens in a goroutine with no error propagation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The detached goroutines have no panic recovery; previously the legacy write ran inline inside the request handler where the apiserver's per-request recover middleware contained any panic, but a panic inside these goroutines is now unrecovered. A panic in any LegacyStorage implementation during an async dual write crashes the entire apiserver process instead of failing one request — four new crash vectors (Create, Delete, Update, DeleteCollection) introduced by moving the calls off the request goroutine.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go the legacy writes for Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection were moved into detached `go func(){ ... }()` goroutines, and none of these goroutines include a `defer recover()`/panic handling wrapper. In Go, an unrecovered panic in any goroutine terminates the entire process, so any panic inside `d.Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection` will crash the apiserver. This risk is directly introduced by the diff’s new async execution.
